question: Describe a situation where maintaining integrity cost you something (personally, professionally, or politically). How did you handle it?

raiseTranscript.text: In my first internship I noticed a teammate had copied code from an open-source repo without attribution for our internal tool. My manager wanted to ship it as-is to hit the deadline. I flagged it and we had to rewrite the module, which delayed the release by three days and I stayed late to help.
I got a lower peer rating that cycle because the team felt I slowed them down. My mentor later told me it was the right call.

raiseNotes: Q: situation where integrity cost you
Internship: spotted copied OSS code, manager wanted to ship
Action: escalated, volunteered to rewrite module
Outcome: 3-day delay, lower peer rating that cycle
Quote: 'mentor told me it was the right call'
Follow-up: asked about personal cost → lower rating acknowledged
junior.raiseFeedback: Raises the bar for junior. The candidate described a concrete ethical shortcut on copied code and accepted a measurable personal cost in peer ratings. They owned the escalation and the extra work without claiming hero status. The story stays within individual scope and shows they learned from the feedback about the rating. Biggest strength is willingness to pay the price rather than rationalize the shortcut.

lowerTranscript.text: Once I found a small calculation error in a report I was submitting. I fixed it even though it meant staying an extra hour and the manager was annoyed about the delay.
Did it affect your review or relationships?
Not really, I just made sure it was correct next time.

lowerNotes: Found calc error in report, fixed it
Outcome: vague 'made sure it was correct next time'
Follow-up: asked about review impact → no clear effect stated
junior.lowerFeedback: Lowers the bar for junior. The example is too minor and the candidate could not articulate any lasting personal or professional cost. They did not show reflection on how the decision affected trust or their standing. The story feels like routine correctness rather than a meaningful integrity trade-off. Biggest gap is absence of observable consequence or learning.

raiseTranscript.text: As tech lead I refused to sign off on a feature that overstated our data freshness to a partner team. It would have helped close a cross-team dependency but risked misleading their roadmap. We delayed the integration by two weeks while we added proper staleness signals.
The partner team escalated to my director and I had to spend extra cycles justifying the decision in two planning meetings. My own launch slipped one sprint.

raiseNotes: Q: integrity cost situation
Refused to sign off on overstated data freshness for partner
Action: added staleness signals, delayed integration
Cost: director escalation, two extra planning meetings, own launch slipped
Quote: 'had to justify the decision in two planning meetings'
Follow-up: asked about cost → director escalation and sprint slip
senior.raiseFeedback: Raises the bar for senior. The candidate protected a partner team from inaccurate data at the cost of their own launch date and political capital with a director. They handled the escalation directly rather than escalating the problem upward. The trade-off is clear and tied to cross-team trust. Biggest strength is treating the cost as expected rather than unfair.

lowerTranscript.text: I pushed back on a PM who wanted to launch without proper testing. We added a few more test cases and it only added a week.
Any fallout with the PM or leadership?
We talked it through and eventually aligned.

lowerNotes: Pushed for more testing against PM preference
Follow-up: asked about fallout → no specific cost described
senior.lowerFeedback: Lowers the bar for senior. The candidate frames the decision as routine process hygiene with minimal cost. No evidence of political or delivery impact is provided. The story does not demonstrate influence without authority or willingness to absorb real trade-offs. Biggest gap is lack of concrete personal or team-level consequence.

raiseTranscript.text: One of my engineers was underperforming on a critical project. HR advised a quick PIP to protect the team metric. I chose a slower coaching path instead, which meant the project missed its quarterly goal and my own bonus was impacted.
Two senior engineers questioned why we were carrying the load. I explained the long-term retention bet and offered to absorb some of their scope. The engineer eventually improved and stayed.

raiseNotes: Q: integrity cost situation
Chose coaching over quick PIP for underperformer
Cost: missed quarterly goal, personal bonus hit
Action: explained retention bet to team, absorbed scope
Outcome: engineer improved and stayed
Follow-up: asked about team response → two seniors questioned decision
manager.raiseFeedback: Raises the bar for manager. The candidate accepted a direct hit to their bonus to give an underperformer a fair development path instead of using a PIP for optics. They owned the team-level impact and absorbed scope to maintain trust. The story shows clear trade-off between short-term results and long-term culture. Biggest strength is treating people development as a measurable cost they were willing to pay.

lowerTranscript.text: I had an engineer who kept missing deadlines. I documented everything and put them on a PIP after the second miss. It was clean and the rest of the team appreciated the clarity.
Did it cost you anything with the team or your leadership?
A couple people asked questions but it resolved quickly.

lowerNotes: Placed engineer on PIP after two misses
Follow-up: asked about cost → vague 'resolved quickly'
manager.lowerFeedback: Lowers the bar for manager. The candidate presents the PIP as a clean process win without acknowledging any development or trust cost. No evidence of coaching effort or willingness to absorb short-term pain for the individual. The story reads as risk avoidance rather than ethical leadership. Biggest gap is absence of personal ownership for the outcome.

raiseTranscript.text: We discovered a legacy product was quietly violating a regional data residency law in one market. Fixing it required pulling the product for six weeks and taking a $4M revenue hit in that quarter. I chose disclosure and remediation over quiet negotiation with regulators.

The CFO and two board members pushed hard for a phased rollout to protect the number. I took the decision to the full board and accepted that my own compensation package would be recalibrated downward for the year.

raiseNotes: Q: integrity cost situation
Legacy product violating data residency law
Action: chose full disclosure and 6-week pull instead of quiet fix
Cost: $4M revenue, CFO/board pushback, personal comp recalibrated
Quote: 'accepted that my own compensation package would be recalibrated'
Follow-up: asked about internal reaction → board-level pushback described
exec.raiseFeedback: Raises the bar for exec. The candidate accepted a material revenue hit and personal compensation impact to correct a compliance violation rather than risk regulatory exposure. They owned the decision at board level and did not delegate the political cost. The story demonstrates long-term judgment over quarterly optics. Biggest strength is treating regulatory integrity as non-negotiable even when it directly affected their own pay.

lowerTranscript.text: We had a minor policy gray area in one region. I asked legal to review and we adjusted the wording before the next audit cycle.
Any business or personal impact from the decision?
It added a little process overhead but kept us clean.

lowerNotes: Minor policy gray area, legal review and wording change
Outcome: 'kept us clean' with little overhead
Follow-up: asked about impact → no material cost stated
exec.lowerFeedback: Lowers the bar for exec. The candidate describes a low-stakes wording adjustment with no visible business or personal cost. The example does not test strategic judgment under ambiguity or willingness to absorb material downside. Biggest gap is lack of any real trade-off at organizational scale.

diagnostic.senior: Names launch slip or director escalation
diagnostic.manager: Names bonus or team goal miss
diagnostic.exec: Names revenue hit and comp adjustment
